The negotiation

Florence, mid-October. Lupu, Ion's dog, has had six puppies. Ion has promised one to Pietro, if the family agrees. In the trattoria, Pietro begins negotiating with Grandma Graziella and his father, Marco.
Grandma, Dad… Grandpa Ion says Lupu has had six puppies. Can I have one?
A dog? In the trattoria? Not a chance. Unless…
Unless?
Unless you promise me you'll take it out every day. Twice a day.
And provided homework comes before the dog. Always.
I promise! I promise everything!
And on condition that it never comes into the kitchen. Never, Pietro. Not even when I'm making ribollita.
And if it rains?
You take it out anyway, provided you put on your raincoat. Otherwise you'll get ill and Grandma will have to take the dog out.
And in case I'm really ill?
In that case Signor Franco will see to it. As long as you don't call it Batman.
All right! Provided Grandpa Ion manages to bring it all the way here.
He'll bring it by train, of course. Unless he decides to come on foot.

1. Purché, a condizione che, a patto che + subjunctive
These three conjunctions introduce a necessary condition ("only if this happens") and take the SUBJUNCTIVE:
Puoi avere il cane, purché te ne occupi tu.
Va bene, a condizione che non entri in cucina.
All right, on condition that it doesn't come into the kitchen.
Lo porti fuori, a patto che ti metta l’impermeabile.
You take it out, provided you put on your raincoat.
"A patto che" sounds a bit like a contract ("on the understanding that…"). "Purché" is the shortest and most used.
2. A meno che (non) + subjunctive
"A meno che" means "unless". The "non" that follows is NOT a real negative and can be left out:
No dog, unless you promise me you'll take it out.
He'll come by train, unless he decides to come on foot.
We'll go out, unless it rains.
Careful: "a meno che tu non venga" = "unless you come", not "unless you don't come". The "non" is purely stylistic.
3. Nel caso in cui, qualora, in caso di
nel caso in cui / nel caso che + subj.
Nel caso in cui piovesse, mettiti l’impermeabile.
qualora + subj.
Qualora il cane entrasse in cucina, sarà punito.
in caso di + noun
In caso di pioggia, la festa è rinviata.
On signs and in regulations: "In caso di emergenza, rompere il vetro" (In case of emergency, break the glass).
4. Basta che, sempre che
Call it whatever you like, as long as you don't call it Batman.
He'll arrive on Saturday, provided the train is on time.
You can stay, as long as you keep quiet.
"Basta che" is very informal and sounds like a sigh: "Fai quello che vuoi, basta che tu sia felice."
5. Altrimenti, se no and the sequence of tenses
"Altrimenti" and "se no" (or "sennò", informal) show what happens if you don't meet the condition. In the past, the subjunctive moves to the imperfetto:
Ti do il cane purché tu lo porti fuori.
Gli avevano dato il cane purché lo portasse fuori.
Mettiti l’impermeabile, altrimenti ti ammali.
Si è messo l’impermeabile, altrimenti si sarebbe ammalato.
Sbrigati, se no perdi il treno.
Si è sbrigato, se no avrebbe perso il treno.
Put your jacket on, otherwise you'll get ill.
In case of rain, the party is postponed.

Il contratto del cane

The negotiation lasted three days and was more complicated than any dealings with the Heritage Authority. Every evening Pietro came home with a new condition to accept. Graziella wanted the dog not to come into the kitchen unless it was invited. Marco wanted homework finished before every walk. Sara, his mother, only wanted the dog not to sleep in Pietro's bed, "unless there's a thunderstorm".

The others had something to say too. Signor Franco was willing to look after the dog, provided it didn't bark during the news. Matei and Giulia agreed, on condition that Lupino didn't eat the workshop's brushes. Viola, who was seventeen months old, set no conditions: every time she heard the word "dog", she said "woof" and clapped her hands. She was, in fact, the only person in the family in favour without reservations.

On the fourth day Pietro went to the workshop with a sheet covered in crossings-out and asked Chiara for help. "You're the one who writes formal letters," he told her. "Will you write me a contract? Then nobody can change the rules afterwards." Chiara put down her brush, took off her glasses and looked at him very seriously. "A real contract?" "Totally real. With signatures."

Chiara worked on it during her lunch break. The result was a two-page document entitled "Agreement for the adoption of a puppy", with numbered articles like a law. Article 1: "Mr Pietro undertakes to take the dog out twice a day, provided it doesn't snow more than ten centimetres." Article 2: "The dog will not enter the kitchen unless Signora Graziella authorises it in writing."

Article 3: "Schoolwork will always come before the dog, on condition that the dog agrees." Article 4: "Should Mr Pietro be ill, Signor Franco will look after the dog, provided he is offered a coffee." Article 5, the last one, added by hand by Bellini, who happened to be passing: "It is forbidden to call the dog Batman, Caravaggio or Bellini."

The contract was signed on Saturday morning, at the workshop, in front of all the open-workshop visitors, who thought it was part of the tour. Pietro, Graziella, Marco, Sara and Signor Franco as "witness" all signed and, in one corner, with a smudge of purple crayon, so did Viola. Chiara added a real stamp, the workshop's. Then she sent a photo of the contract to Sibiu.

From Sibiu, Ion's reply came ten minutes later, translated by Ilinca: "I accept all the conditions. I'll bring the puppy to Florence by train, provided nobody asks me to take a plane. I'll arrive on the first of November, provided the Austrian railways do their duty. In case of delay, it's their fault, not mine."

In Sibiu, meanwhile, Ion and Doina had to choose which of the six puppies to send to Italy. Ion wanted the biggest, "because in Florence you need a serious dog". Doina wanted the female, "because females are calmer". In the end they let Lupu himself choose. The old dog sniffed his pups one by one, stopped next to the smallest, the grey one with enormous ears, and nudged it gently with his nose towards Ion. The decision was made.

The problem was that, on international trains, dogs have to travel with papers, vaccinations, a microchip and an approved pet carrier. Ion spent two weeks going between vets and offices, filling in forms in Romanian, Hungarian and German. "If I'd known," he told Doina one evening, "I'd have brought a cat. Cats don't need a passport." "Cats have them too," Doina replied. "But Pietro wanted a dog."

The journey was long. In Budapest a ticket inspector wanted to see all the puppy's papers, one by one, and Ion showed them with a stationmaster's pride. In Vienna the puppy cried for an hour, until Doina picked it up and sang it Viorica's lullaby. From then on it slept all the way to Venice, as long as Doina kept singing. Doina sang for seven hours.

On the first of November, at eight in the evening, the train from Venice arrived at Santa Maria Novella station only four minutes late. Ion got off first, with a light blue plastic carrier in one hand and a folder full of documents in the other. Behind him was Doina, with her usual three bags of food. Waiting on the platform were Pietro, Graziella, Matei, Giulia, Viola and half the workshop.

Pietro knelt down on the platform and opened the carrier. Inside was a grey and white puppy, with ears that were too big and the yellow eyes of his father Lupu. The puppy looked at Pietro for a long moment, its head tilted to one side. Then it jumped into his arms and licked his face, from chin to forehead. Pietro couldn't say a word. He was laughing and crying at the same time.

"What are you going to call him?" asked Giulia. Pietro had thought about it for three weeks, respecting article 5 of the contract. "His name is Lupino," he said. "Little Lupu. That way, even though he's in Florence, he won't forget where he comes from." Ion, who didn't understand Italian but understood the word "Lupu" perfectly well, had to blow his nose into his handkerchief for quite a while.

On the first night, by a strange coincidence, a violent thunderstorm broke over Florence. At two o'clock Sara opened Pietro's bedroom door to check. Lupino was asleep in the bed, next to the pillow, and Pietro had his arms round him. Sara was about to say something, then heard a clap of thunder and remembered her own words: "unless there's a thunderstorm". She closed the door without a sound. The contract, after all, had been respected.

The contract was respected almost perfectly. Pietro took Lupino out twice a day, even in the rain, provided he had his raincoat. Homework came before the dog, unless the dog was whining at the door, which happened often. And Lupino never came into the kitchen. Never. Except on Sundays, when Graziella made ribollita and, without telling anyone, let a little piece of bread fall under the table.

"And article 2?" Marco, who had seen her, asked one day. Graziella shrugged. "Article 2 says the dog doesn't come into the kitchen unless I authorise it," she replied. "I've authorised it. In writing." And she pointed to a little note stuck on the fridge, in her handwriting: "Lupino: authorised on Sundays. Provided nobody finds out."

That evening, at the workshop, Bellini read the contract hanging on the wall, where Chiara had framed it like a historical document. He smiled. Then he took his pen and, under article 5, added one last line in his elegant handwriting: "Article 6: The dog may visit the workshop on Saturdays, on condition that it looks and doesn't touch anything." The following Saturday, Lupino sat down in front of the glass, next to Davide, and stayed perfectly still for exactly five minutes.
